design_detail: One-paragraph case report in the BMJ's 'Drug points' column (25 February 1995, p. 504, about 350 words and four references, printed beside two unrelated drug points): three urologists at Stepping Hill Hospital, Stockport, describe one young man who came to them in acute urinary retention after taking ecstasy tablets, and add a paragraph of textbook pharmacology about the nerve supply of the bladder. There is no investigation beyond the clinical examination and management described: no drug testing, no analysis of the tablets, no hormone or sodium measurement, no urodynamic study, no imaging and no stated follow-up after the hospital stay.
can_establish: That one healthy 19-year-old man was treated for acute urinary retention after reporting that he had taken 15 ecstasy tablets in the previous 36 hours, that catheterisation for 36 hours resolved it and it did not recur, and that his doctors knew of no earlier report of retention of urine with this drug.
cannot_establish: That MDMA caused the retention (the tablets were never analysed, no drug test was done, and no measurement in this man supports the proposed mechanism); how often retention or lesser difficulty passing urine happens in people who take MDMA; what amount, if any, is involved; or whether the effect would recur, since no rechallenge and no follow-up are reported.

sample.recruitment: One man referred to a hospital urology service; how the case came to be written up is not stated (p. 504).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not applicable: a single referred case.
sample.demographics: A healthy 19-year-old man. Weight, ethnicity, occupation, alcohol use and medical history beyond 'healthy' are not reported.
sample.attrition: Not applicable. No follow-up period is stated; the report says only that no further retention occurred.
sample.selection_effects: A case is published because it is unusual and because the authors could think of a cause. Nothing can be inferred from it about how often this happens, and cases in which young people in retention had taken the same drug without the link being drawn, or had taken it without any trouble passing urine, would not be reported.

exposure.measurement: Self-report only, given in two stages: an initial history of drug use, then a later admission of the quantity. No urine or blood drug screen, and no analysis of the tablets, is reported. The urinalysis mentioned is a routine examination of the urine, not a drug test (p. 504).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: As reported by the man himself, not as anything the authors measured: for the 12 months before admission, one or two ecstasy tablets once or twice a week, usually at parties; then 15 tablets during the 36 hours before admission. Earlier in his life he had used amphetamine and smoked cannabis. The content and strength of the tablets are unknown, and the time between the last tablet and the start of the retention is not given.
exposure.polysubstance: He reported earlier use of amphetamine and cannabis but said he had used only ecstasy in the previous 12 months. Alcohol and any other substance taken during the 36 hours are not mentioned, and no toxicology was done to check.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; he was in retention on arrival, 24 hours after it began.

comparison.controls: None. One person, one occasion, no comparison group and no comparison occasion.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No measurement of this man's bladder function before the episode, and no information on earlier difficulty passing urine, prostate or urethral problems, constipation, fluid intake or dehydration on the day.

outcomes.instruments: Clinical: history, general examination, a painful palpable bladder, examination of the urine, and urethral catheterisation with free drainage. No residual volume, flow rate, ultrasound or blood test is reported (p. 504).
outcomes.validity_norms: Acute retention of urine relieved by catheterisation is a clinically unambiguous event. Nothing else in the report was measured.
outcomes.operationalization: The outcome is the clinical event itself: 24 hours of inability to pass urine, relieved by a catheter left in for 36 hours, with no recurrence while under the authors' care.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; the treating doctors wrote the report.

analysis.effect_sizes: None. A single narrative case with no numerical outcome and no statistics. The only quantities are the clinical course (24 hours of retention before referral, catheter removed after 36 hours), the reported pattern of use (one or two tablets once or twice a week for 12 months) and the reported quantity before admission (15 tablets in 36 hours).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not applicable to a case report.
analysis.selective_reporting: The report gives no toxicology, no residual urine volume, no timing between the last tablet and the retention, and no length of follow-up; whether these were absent or simply not printed cannot be told from a column item of this length.

interpretation_gap.results_show: One young man was in acute urinary retention for 24 hours and was catheterised for 36 hours, after reporting 15 ecstasy tablets in the preceding 36 hours; examination and urinalysis were otherwise normal and the retention did not come back.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The authors write that his use of the drug "almost certainly led to acute urinary retention" (p. 504), reasoning from the bladder's nerve supply and from MDMA being an alpha-adrenergic agonist; they recommend that misuse of synthetic amphetamines be considered in young people with unexplained urinary retention, which is a reasonable clinical suggestion. The photograph printed beside the item carries a caption presenting retention of urine as something large amounts of ecstasy can cause, which is a general causal statement drawn from one case. Nothing in this man was measured to support the alpha-adrenergic account: no drug was identified in him, no tablet was analysed, and no alternative cause was ruled out beyond a normal general examination and examination of the urine.

timeline.event: Greer and Tolbert's account of MDMA given in a clinical setting, cited here (reference 3) as the source of the only earlier urological complication the authors knew of, urgency of passing urine
Worsley and colleagues, cited here (reference 4), had reported bladder outflow obstruction after intravenous amphetamine
This case: acute retention of urine after reported ecstasy use, presented as the first of its kind known to the authors

replication.where_it_stands: No study with a comparison group, and no series, on difficulty passing urine after MDMA was among the papers read for this card; the question rests on isolated reports and on pharmacological reasoning. The related and much better studied effect of MDMA on water and sodium balance is covered by the controlled studies in this library (sc_baggott_2016, sc_henry_1998) and by the poison-centre and case series on low blood sodium (sc_hartung_2002, sc_rosenson_2007, sc_campbell_2008); those papers do not report urine volumes either.

funding.funder: Not reported. The BMJ's 'Drug points' column carried no funding statement.
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported; no competing-interests statement appears with the item.
funding.affiliations_note: Three clinicians at Stepping Hill Hospital, Stockport, writing about a patient they treated. The item is a clinical report by the treating team, not independent research.

what_would_settle_it: A study that asks a defined group of people who use MDMA about difficulty passing urine after use, with a comparison period or comparison group and with measurement of what they took, or a series of people presenting in retention who are drug tested on arrival; either would turn an isolated report into a rate and show whether the association survives testing.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Appraised with the JBI checklist, as the round brief directs for case reports; most items do not apply to one person. The clinical event is described by the team that treated it and is not in doubt, but the risk of bias is high for any statement about cause: the drug was never identified in this man or in the tablets, no measurement supports the proposed alpha-adrenergic mechanism, no other cause was excluded beyond a normal examination, and a single published case carries no information about how often this happens. It may be cited, as one reported case, for the fact that acute retention of urine has been described after someone took a large number of ecstasy tablets, for how it was managed and for the authors' suggestion that this be considered in young people in unexplained retention. It may not be cited for a causal effect of MDMA on the bladder, for a mechanism, for any frequency, or for a relation to the amount taken.

key_findings.finding: A healthy 19-year-old man was referred with a 24-hour history of acute retention of urine; apart from a painful palpable bladder, general examination and examination of the urine showed nothing abnormal.
key_findings.locator: Urinary retention with misuse of 'ecstasy', 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: A urethral catheter was inserted and removed after 36 hours on free drainage, and no further retention of urine occurred.
key_findings.locator: Urinary retention with misuse of 'ecstasy', 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: No length of follow-up is given, so 'no further retention' covers an unstated period.

key_findings.finding: He reported that for the 12 months before admission he had used only ecstasy, one or two tablets once or twice a week, usually at parties, and later said he had taken 15 tablets during the 36 hours before admission; earlier in his life he had used amphetamine and smoked cannabis.
key_findings.locator: Urinary retention with misuse of 'ecstasy', 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: All of this is the man's own account, disclosed in two stages. No drug screen and no analysis of the tablets is reported, so what he took is unknown.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the only urological complication of this drug noted before, as far as they knew, was urgency of passing urine, citing a 1986 account of MDMA given in a clinical setting.
key_findings.locator: Urinary retention with misuse of 'ecstasy', 2nd paragraph; reference 3
key_findings.note: Second-hand; the cited source was not read.

key_findings.finding: The mechanism the authors propose is pharmacological reasoning, not a measurement: beta-adrenergic nerves supply the detrusor muscle and alpha-adrenergic fibres the trigone and bladder neck, blocking alpha fibres relaxes the bladder neck while stimulating them can close it, and MDMA is described as a potent alpha-adrenergic agonist.
key_findings.locator: Urinary retention with misuse of 'ecstasy', 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: No receptor binding, no measurement in this man and no citation for MDMA's alpha-adrenergic potency is given at this point in the text.

key_findings.finding: The authors recommend that misuse of synthetic amphetamines be considered in cases of unexplained urinary retention in young people.
key_findings.locator: Urinary retention with misuse of 'ecstasy', last paragraph

key_findings.finding: The complications of the drug listed in the report, taken from two cited sources (references 1 and 2) rather than from this case, are trismus (jaw clenching), loss of appetite, chest pain, aching muscles, sweating and high fever. [Note to keep: second-hand; the cited sources were not read. Drop the note's sentence calling low blood sodium 'the best documented cause of serious harm': it is not from this source, and the item calls neither source a review.]
key_findings.locator: Urinary retention with misuse of 'ecstasy', 2nd paragraph; references 1 and 2
key_findings.note: Second-hand; the cited sources were not read. Low blood sodium, the best documented cause of serious harm with this drug, is not among them.

reporting_issues.issue: No drug testing of any kind is reported: the urine analysis is not described as a drug test, and no test of the man or of the tablets for MDMA or anything else is mentioned.
reporting_issues.consequence: The exposure on which the whole report rests is unverified, so the substance involved is unknown. (The original's statement about what ecstasy tablets of that period contained is not from this source.)

reporting_issues.issue: The timing is never reconciled: he was referred with a 24-hour history of retention and said he had taken 15 tablets during the 36 hours before admission, so, if referral was at admission, the retention began within that period, about 12 hours into it; when he took the last tablet is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: The interval between taking the drug and the retention, which is what a causal reading depends on, cannot be worked out.

reporting_issues.issue: The reported quantity, 15 tablets in 36 hours, is many times his described usual pattern of one or two tablets once or twice a week, and the authors do not comment on the discrepancy or on what else might have been taken during those 36 hours.
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether the episode followed an unusual quantity, an unusual tablet or something else entirely cannot be told, and any dose-related reading of the case is unsupported.

reporting_issues.issue: The causal statement in the text is strong (the misuse "almost certainly led to acute urinary retention"), while the evidence offered for it is textbook pharmacology and the absence of another finding on examination.
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers of the item, and of the photograph caption beside it, may take a general causal fact from a single unverified case.

reporting_issues.issue: No measurement of bladder function is reported: no residual volume on catheterisation, no flow study, no imaging and no later review.
reporting_issues.consequence: The severity of the retention and whether bladder function returned fully cannot be judged, and the case cannot be compared with others.
